extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science communicators, journal and university press officers, and journalists interested in press-release/news accuracy
extracted.subtask_description: Coding and analysing the content of health- and biomedical-related press releases, their source journal articles, and resulting news stories to detect exaggeration, caveats, justifications, and advice; and to measure associations with news uptake. Uses a structured content-analysis protocol and statistical inference for clustered news outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health advice coding (maximum level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each source was coded for maximum level of advice out of four possible categories: no advice, implicit advice, explicit advice but not to the reader/general public, or explicit advice to the reader/general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: implicit ('for adults with a BMI greater than 35 kg/m2…permanent calorie reductions of more than 500 calories per day would be needed…'); explicit but not to reader ('clinicians must exercise caution in their use of aflibercept'); explicit to reader ('patients who are at increased risk of cardiovascular events should consider starting statin treatment promptly and continuing it long-term'). A press-release/journal-article/news set was included in the advice analysis only if at least one source contained implicit or explicit advice (N specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal-claim strength coding (7-level scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Main statements of findings were coded for strength on seven levels: no statement, statement of no relationship, correlational, ambiguous, conditional causal, can cause, and causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code the main statement in the title and first two sentences for press releases/news; for journal articles use the abstract and discussion. Focus the analysis on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal studies; exclude qualitative, intervention, or simulation designs. The first two sentences are used because the main claims are typically stated first and most influence readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference from non-human research
rubrics_metrics.description: For journal articles based on non-human samples (animals, cells, or simulations), code whether the press release and news state findings as explicitly non-human, implicitly human, or explicitly human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and counts provided; low N limited further analyses. This captures whether non-human research is translated as human-relevant in PRs/news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat presence coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code presence or absence of caveats for causal/correlational statements and for explicit advice in press releases (and corresponding news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of caveats: 'We still need more research to clarify whether vitamin D directly prevents bowel cancer...' Caveats were rare; to increase power datasets from journal and university press releases were combined. Analyses report odds ratios for caveats appearing in news when present in press releases and examine caveats' association with news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification presence coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code whether justifications for causal statements or for advice are present in the press release (and news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications are statements that justify the strength of conclusions (e.g. 'Unlike previous researchers [authors] looked at children from all social backgrounds'). Presence/absence coded only where relevant (specified Ns). Analysed for association with news uptake and transmission to news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'exaggeration'
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is defined as claims or advice in press releases or news that are coded at a level above any of the associated statements in the peer-reviewed journal article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational definition records 'message creep' beyond the journal article text; it does not attempt to judge whether the journal article itself contains exaggeration. Thus exaggeration is measured relative to the journal article baseline, not an external standard of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding window / location for main claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Main claims for press releases and news were coded from the title and the first two sentences; for journal articles coding used the abstract and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: main claims are typically stated first and likely to have greatest influence on readers. This protocol focuses on the main statements rather than supporting text further down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion/exclusion criteria for causal-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Include only studies that are correlational (cross-sectional or longitudinal) when analysing causal claims; exclude qualitative, intervention, or simulation designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures comparison of causal language where causal inference is not warranted by study design; Ns for this subset are specified in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: linked PR–article–news set
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses compare statements across linked triplets (press release, peer-reviewed article, and associated news stories); exaggeration is assessed relative to the journal article in each set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some analyses only include sets where at least one news story exists; news articles are clustered under press releases (several news articles per PR) and clustering is adjusted in statistical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding instrument: comprehensive question set
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding used a set list of 191 questions in the coding sheet focusing primarily on advice, causal claims, and conclusions about humans from non-human research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many questions did not apply to every press release depending on content. Coding each set took 3–4 hours; full coding sheets and instructions are available in the open data repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double coding and reliability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomly select a portion of press releases and associated news for independent double-coding to estimate concordance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study 147 press releases (27.5%) and 144 news stories (24.7%) were double-coded, yielding a concordance rate of 98.3% (κ = 0.97). The paper notes a trade-off between more double-coding and increasing sample size, recommending the latter for reliability when concordance is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure 'news uptake' as whether a press release has resulting news articles (presence/absence) and count the number of news stories per press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare proportions of PRs with and without news; use bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals and standard inferential tests for news uptake comparisons (no clustering). Also compare mean number of news stories per PR between groups and report CIs for differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis methods for clustered data
rubrics_metrics.description: Use generalized estimating equations (GEE) to estimate percentages, 95% confidence intervals, and odds ratios while adjusting for clustering of several news articles per press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For news uptake comparisons (no clustering issue) use bootstrapped CIs. Report odds ratios with CIs for associations between PR exaggeration and news exaggeration, and for caveats/justifications transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection and scope criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Select press releases based on possible relevance to human health, psychology or neuroscience from a specified set of leading journals for a defined time period (here: entire year 2011 from Lancet, BMJ, Science, Nature, Nature Neuroscience, Nature Immunology, Nature Medicine, Nature Genetics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect press releases from public repositories (journal pages, EurekAlert, press sites). Identify associated news articles from Nexis, BBC.co.uk, Reuters, and Google searches. Note limitations: not all journals issue press releases and the sample of journals is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline decision: do not re-evaluate journal-article accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to judge whether the peer-reviewed journal article itself contains exaggeration; use the journal article's statements as the baseline for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that many journal articles might already contain exaggeration and that a different approach (expert re-evaluation of each paper) would likely find higher total exaggeration rates. This is an explicit methodological choice shaping the definition of exaggeration used.
